::: {.apr}

Many engineering organizations are moving toward the same pattern: software approves small, low-risk pull requests, and people review the rest. We analyzed twelve public write-ups of the pattern, most of them written by the organizations themselves, and extracted 26 recurring themes. For each theme we counted how many of the sources mention it.

In the charts, each bar is a count of sources out of 12, drawn in two shades as keyed in the legend. "Substantial" means the source gives the theme a section, a specific mechanism or a number; "brief mention" means a sentence or a clear implication. The number in brackets is the substantial count. Hover a bar to see which sources.

Eleven of the twelve sources raise the same problem: AI-assisted engineers produce code faster than people can review it, and ten of them make that the main argument. The evidence is mostly throughput numbers. Meta reports significant lines per human-landed diff up 105.9% in a year and diffs per developer up 51%. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September. At Assembled, median time to first review went from 3.5 hours (December 2025) to over 16 hours (May 2026). PostHog's monthly PR count went from 1,441 to 4,725 between January and June with headcount up about 10%. Tessl counts over 1,200 agent-written PRs a week, Mirage reports code-change throughput up 146% in a year (adjusted for headcount), Ona's engineers open 10.8 PRs a week each, and Rewind counts about forty PRs a day competing for senior attention.

> Humans simply don’t have the time or mental capacity to properly review the volume of AI-generated code.
>
> — Intercom


Two further motives come up less often. Eight sources argue that human review is itself imperfect, and that on routine changes it turns into rubber-stamping. Intercom notes that the product changes that caused its past outages "were all reviewed and approved by humans"; Rewind calls an unexamined approval "a rubber stamp wearing the costume of a control"; Mirage says reviewing many low-risk changes "leads to review fatigue". Six sources point to the cost of waiting on the author: Customer.io opens on "the cognitive weight of waiting", and Ona describes authors deep in another task by the time approval arrives. Customer.io is the one source that does not describe a capacity bottleneck; its case rests on the author's wait.

Every source sorts changes by risk and gives the low-risk ones a lighter path. The tiers differ in form. Rewind grades every PR low, medium or high from what its reviewers found. Zalando rates each PR at creation using rules derived from its production incidents. Mirage has two classes, set by a published list of file paths. Anthropic's Claude Code team uses three tiers that require zero, one or two human approvals, set by the change and not by the author, with lighter paths only for trusted authors. Ona writes a six-criterion policy that must hold in full, Customer.io sorts changes into routine, structural and critical, and Meta thresholds a risk score and requires its LLM reviewer to find every change in a safe category.

Eleven of the twelve also name categories of change that stay with humans, some only in passing. The matrix below counts the ones that name specific categories. A filled cell means the post says so explicitly.

Size is the other common gate. Seven sources cap or measure diff size, and the numbers cluster: Ona and Assembled use under 1,000 lines; PostHog uses under 500 lines and 20 files. Customer.io measures lines, files and component boundaries but doesn't publish a cutoff. Intercom's agent refuses PRs it judges too big, complex or broad. Meta uses a review-effort score rather than lines.

One source disputes the proxy. Rewind argues diff size says little about risk, and sets a roughly 10,000-line ceiling only as a limit on human attention, "not as a risk signal".

> A twelve-line database migration that adds an index to a fifty-million-row table is one of the most dangerous things you can ship [...] A three-thousand-line PR that regenerates an API client from an updated schema is, in risk terms, nothing.
>
> — Rewind


PostHog's blog (read via a summary) treats line count as only a rough proxy for quality, while its newsletter piece describes the 500-line cap.

### How the review is done

The first chart in this part also shows how the review itself is built. Seven sources use several narrowly scoped reviewers in place of one: Anthropic's review agents "do not share biases and blindspots", OpenAI uses domain specialists per infrastructure area, Intercom has sub-agents for intent, safety and logic, Assembled runs Codex and Claude Code independently, PostHog's qa-swarm spawns four reviewers, Tessl configures separate review "lenses", and Rewind convenes a "council" of a dozen or more.

Nine sources keep the final decision in deterministic code rather than in the model's judgment. Rewind sends findings to a unit-tested verdict engine ("The judgment is AI; the gate is not a vibe"). Assembled combines fixed rules, such as the 1,000-line cap, with LLM-based policies. PostHog runs deterministic gates first, and its shared prompt says the LLM "can tighten gates but never loosen". Mirage classifies by file path in CI, and any AI verdict that isn't a clear approval defaults to "request changes". In Meta's system any failed check routes the diff to a human.

"The AI approves PRs" covers three arrangements in these sources. Counts here are by source, and each source is placed in the arrangement it describes for its main system.

```{=html}
<div class="lanes"><div class="lane"><div class="lhead"><b>AI approves, human merges or ships</b><span class="lcount">4</span></div><p class="small">The bot clears the review requirement; a person still presses the button.</p><div class="chips"><span class="chip">PostHog</span><span class="chip">Rewind</span><span class="chip">Ona</span><span class="chip">Zalando</span></div></div><div class="lane"><div class="lhead"><b>A slice lands with no human at all</b><span class="lcount">5</span></div><p class="small">For some class of change, nobody looks before it ships.</p><div class="chips"><span class="chip">Meta</span><span class="chip">Anthropic</span><span class="chip">OpenAI</span><span class="chip">Intercom</span><span class="chip">Tessl</span></div></div><div class="lane"><div class="lhead"><b>Post doesn&#x27;t say</b><span class="lcount">3</span></div><p class="small">Approval is automated, but who merges isn&#x27;t stated.</p><div class="chips"><span class="chip">Customer.io</span><span class="chip">Assembled</span><span class="chip">Mirage</span></div></div></div>
```


Ona and Rewind are the most explicit about why the human click matters. Ona: "a person always clicks the merge button", and that click is what its SOC 2 audit sees. Rewind: "Auto-approve is not auto-merge", and a PR authored by a bot "can never be merged without a human clicking the button". Both use the human merge as the answer to separation of duties. At Zalando the bot approves and "the author of the PR can thus choose to merge", and PostHog's planning issue says agent-authored PRs "still always need a human review".

Five sources let some class of change land with no human at all. Meta lets bot-authored diffs that pass every gate land after a short delay in which a human can still reject them, and human-authored diffs that pass a stricter second step need no review at all, "not even deferred". Intercom says 497 PRs went "fully autonomous" in four weeks, "with Claude writing the code and our AI approval system reviewing, approving, and shipping to production". On the Claude Code team, low-risk changes (docs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flag) need no human approval once automated review and security checks are green, though "an agent's approval never counts as a person's" for the medium and high slots. OpenAI's harness-engineering post says of one internal repo that "humans may review pull requests, but aren't required to", and that agents often squash and merge their own PRs; the post says this "should not be assumed to generalize". Tessl reports about 75% of its PRs merging without human review, which it defines as merging without a human "correcting the agent or discussing the engineering".

Six sources keep an opt-in or override: Intercom says "any engineer can request a human review on any change, at any time", and in Rewind a `/request-jedi-review` comment stands the bot down. Five keep the reviewer independent of the author. PostHog's wording is that "the agent that wrote the code can’t be the one that reviews it", and Mirage requires a human who is not the author for its high-risk class.

The most common safeguards are about how the system is introduced and watched, not about the model. Seven sources started in shadow mode or a pilot: Rewind spent its first week over 400+ repositories, with 90% agreement with human reviewers as the bar to go live, Intercom piloted on 100+ PRs, and Tessl ran old and new reviewers side by side on every PR for a week. Nine keep an audit trail of every AI verdict (Intercom: "Every AI-approved PR is labelled, logged, and queryable"; PostHog dumps a JSON artifact for every run, with the gate results and the verdict's reasoning). Nine run a loop where human reactions tune the policy, such as Intercom's helpful or not-helpful marks on review comments and the Claude Code team's daily eval built from past incidents and reverts. Ona states the thesis directly: "The governance model matters more than the AI model."

Two sources check approvals after the fact. Mirage's weekly review covers "the full population (not a sample)" of AI-approved merges, with a human signing off each week's list. Anthropic's security post says every approval is logged "and a risk-weighted sample is reviewed by humans".

Seven address a compliance regime. Intercom engaged an auditor before scaling and maps to SOC 2, HIPAA and several ISO standards; Mirage designed its policy for SOC 2 CC8.1 with its auditors and publishes the policy text; Rewind brought its GRC lead in "at the start, not the end"; Ona treats the human merge click as the SOC 2 approval event. Meta excludes SOX-scoped code from automation.

Five put the approval rules themselves under change control. In Rewind the policy file is CODEOWNERS-protected and "the bot never edits its own prompts or policy". In Mirage the classification script is itself high-risk and changes to it need the CTO. In Ona even swapping the model needs sign-off from the Head of Product Design and Engineering.

Six mention a production-side safety net, such as feature flags, rollback and monitoring, but only two (Anthropic and Intercom) discuss it at length. The Claude Code team lists a merge queue, flags that turn off without a deploy, staged releases and an on-call rotation, and says "everything is reversible". Intercom observes that most of its largest outages weren't caused by product-code changes at all.

The least-covered safeguard is the adversary. Only three sources (Anthropic, PostHog and Rewind) consider a malicious or compromised author or agent. Anthropic describes an incident agent that, after a model upgrade, asked another agent to push a fix, and a human gate stopped it. PostHog's planning issue describes checking out the base branch instead of the PR, "otherwise PR could rewrite its own approval logic", closing a trick in which a benign PR is stacked onto a malicious branch, and dismissing the bot's approval on any later push. Rewind lists "the bot approves a malicious PR" among thirteen failure modes in its risk assessment.



The two PostHog posts disagree: the 9 July newsletter says StampHog stamps "roughly 1 in 3" of the main repo's merged PRs over a quarter; the 28 July blog says 20%. They may measure different windows. Tessl's 75% is the highest figure, but it counts PRs merged without a human correcting the agent or discussing the engineering, which is narrower than "approved by software". Ona reports a before-and-after effect but no share, and Anthropic, OpenAI and Mirage report none.

### Speed

Ten sources report speed or throughput gains, and six give a latency number.

```{=html}
<div class="column-page"><div class="scroll"><table class="plain"><thead><tr><th>Who</th><th>Measure</th><th>Before</th><th>After</th><th>What it compares</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Ona</th><td>Median time to first approval</td><td class="nw">2h 49m</td><td class="nw">3.8 min</td><td class="small">Human-authored PRs; 4-week windows before and after; lead time also fell 74%.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Customer.io</th><td>Median merge time</td><td class="nw">3.5 hours</td><td class="nw">33 min</td><td class="small">AI-approved PRs vs the pre-system baseline; about 500 PRs over 3 months.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Intercom</th><td>Time to approval at p75</td><td class="nw">baseline</td><td class="nw">6 to 16x faster</td><td class="small">Controlled pilot of 100+ PRs.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Assembled</th><td>Median auto-review time</td><td class="nw">16h+ to first review (May)</td><td class="nw">8 min</td><td class="small">Different quantities: queue wait before, review duration after.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Meta</th><td>Median time to close</td><td class="nw">human-reviewed diffs</td><td class="nw">&#x27;over 330%&#x27; lower</td><td class="small">Difference-in-differences vs human-reviewed diffs; paper&#x27;s own phrasing.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Zalando</th><td>PR lead time</td><td class="nw">baseline</td><td class="nw">20 to 40% lower</td><td class="small">Compared with all PRs; no baseline period given.</td></tr></tbody></table></div></div>
```


No source reports a slowdown. Ona's is the clearest case: a step change on the day the bot approved its first PR, with a human still doing the merge, which Ona reads as evidence that "the approval wait was the real blocker".

### Safety

Eight sources report a revert, incident or bug number. This is every safety-flavoured number in the corpus, and what it actually covers.

```{=html}
<div class="column-page"><div class="scroll"><table class="plain"><thead><tr><th>Who</th><th>What they report</th><th>Covers</th><th>Caveat</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Meta</th><td>Revert rate 1/3, incident rate 1/50 of non-RADAR diffs</td><td class="nw">Auto-approved diffs</td><td class="small">Not randomised; approved diffs are the low-risk ones by construction (the paper says so under internal validity).</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Intercom</th><td>0 reverts in a 100+ PR pilot</td><td class="nw">Auto-approved PRs</td><td class="small">Small n; the 0.53% vs 5.39% revert figures cover all AI-authored code, not only approved PRs.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Rewind</th><td>0 reverts, 0 incidents; ~99% agreement with human reviewers</td><td class="nw">Auto-approved PRs</td><td class="small">One shadow week plus one live week; the post itself says 'directional'.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Assembled</th><td>Reverts steady at 0.8% per PR; bugs reported −27%</td><td class="nw">Whole org</td><td class="small">Three weeks; bugs lag, as the post says.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">PostHog</th><td>Revert share 0.2% (June 2026)</td><td class="nw">Whole monorepo</td><td class="small">Not split by approval path; read via a summary. A later fix PR reports the bot approving PRs its own policy said to refuse.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Anthropic</th><td>Claude Code: reverted share of merged PRs down 40%+ (Jun to Sep). ~⅓ of past claude.ai incident bugs would now be caught</td><td class="nw">Whole Claude Code repos; a retrospective</td><td class="small">No control group, and the window overlaps model releases. Nothing specific to approved PRs.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">OpenAI</th><td>~9 in 10 AI review comments flag valid issues</td><td class="nw">Review comments</td><td class="small">Precision of comments, not safety of approvals; relayed by Pragmatic Engineer. Its own post gives no safety numbers.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Tessl</th><td>91% of review findings were real defects</td><td class="nw">Review findings</td><td class="small">Precision of the reviewer, not outcomes; no revert or incident figure for PRs merged without review.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Zalando</th><td>No safety figure</td><td class="nw">—</td><td class="small">Reports lead time and share only.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Mirage</th><td>No safety figure</td><td class="nw">—</td><td class="small">Publishes policy and controls, no outcome metrics.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Customer.io</th><td>No safety figure in the text</td><td class="nw">—</td><td class="small">Search snippets said 'zero incidents across 500 PRs'; not found on the page.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Ona</th><td>No safety figure</td><td class="nw">—</td><td class="small">Reports only speed and throughput.</td></tr></tbody></table></div></div>
```


Only three sources measure the PRs the system approved: Meta, Intercom (a pilot of about a hundred) and Rewind (about a week). Meta's own validity section is the most careful in the set: diffs are not randomly assigned, so a low revert rate on auto-approved diffs is partly built in, since those are the diffs chosen for being low-risk. Nine sources say something about the limits of their own evidence or system. Assembled calls its results "observational results from a rollout, not a randomized trial", Rewind asks readers to "read them as directional", and Tessl reports where its previous reviewer was better. The Claude Code team says it doesn't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when revert numbers move. A PostHog fix PR is the most direct: it says StampHog "approves pull requests that its own written review policy says to refuse or escalate", and that approvals rose as incoming PRs got larger and riskier.

Five report cost: Assembled about \$3.57 per review attempt, Rewind about \$0.73 per PR (over \$12 for large ones), PostHog about \$300 a month for StampHog, Tessl about 35% less per PR than its previous AI reviewer, and Anthropic only that costs will rise with throughput. Four give a concrete case of the AI catching something a human might not. Intercom's agent flagged a one-line copy change that contradicted a validation elsewhere in the codebase, Customer.io describes an embedded struct that would have leaked PII to an external service, and Tessl cites a customer's Swift app where its reviewer found an API key header forwarded across an HTTP redirect.

### Side effects on how people write PRs

Five sources report that the policy changed how engineers write PRs. Ona: large unfocused changes trip the criteria, so engineers "gravitate toward smaller, focused PRs". Intercom: refusing big PRs gives "a direct, positive incentive" to ship small ones. Assembled: to qualify, PRs started arriving with testing evidence and screenshots. Zalando: PRs are now split into quick low-risk ones and slower medium-risk ones, where before such changes were mixed together.

Three sources treat the same mechanism as a risk. Assembled: "our engineers ended up shaping PRs for the approval policy, so whatever the policy rewards, you get more of." Ona's answer is that engineers shouldn't classify their own changes, and automation "removes the temptation to game the system". Intercom takes up the worry about optimizing a ">50% AI-approved" metric and argues it isn't one.

Assembled reports two results nobody else does. A policy that is too strict fails quietly: engineers try it twice, get rejected and stop asking, so the time savings and the feedback both disappear. And throughput on large PRs, which the bot mostly doesn't approve, rose 3.5x. Their explanation is that reviewers no longer get buried in small PRs, so the ones that reach them get real attention.

## Sources and limits

All twelve sources include a document written by the organization itself, though OpenAI's account of company-wide practice and part of PostHog's reach us secondhand (see below). Together they are 18 documents, published between November 2025 and October 2026; 15 of the 18 appeared from April 2026 on.

### How far the evidence goes

- **Every source describes a system that is running.** None reports turning it off, and write-ups of abandoned systems wouldn't appear in a search like this one.
- **The windows are short.** Ona compares two four-week windows, Assembled has three weeks, Rewind has one live week. Bugs reported lag the PRs that cause them.
- **Four of the twelve sell AI development tools** (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ona, Tessl). That doesn't make them wrong, but they have a reason to report this well.
- **The sources are not fully independent.** Intercom is cited by both Anthropic and Rewind. Part of the "many companies" signal is a few companies reading each other.
- **Safe PRs are safe partly by selection.** Approved PRs were picked for being low-risk, so low revert rates on them are partly circular. Meta says this in its paper; most others don't.
- **Some evidence is secondhand.** OpenAI's own post covers one internal repo; the company-wide practice comes from two Pragmatic Engineer articles. PostHog's 10,000-PR blog was read through a summary, so no quotes from it are used beyond what the newsletter piece and GitHub issue support.
- **Customer.io's "zero incidents across 500 PRs"** appeared in search snippets but not in the page text, so it isn't counted.
- **The coding is one reader's.** Two levels (substantial, brief), one coder. The note on every cell in the appendix gives the evidence so it can be checked.
- **Scope.** Vendor products that offer auto-approval (documentation, not experience reports) are not counted.

## Outside the corpus

These turned up while gathering sources. They are not coded in the charts above.

- **Vercel.** A post titled "58% of PRs in our largest monorepo merge without human review" (6 April 2026, according to third-party coverage) is cited by secondary sources, which report an LLM risk classifier and 671 low-risk PRs merged with no revert. Its URL returns a 404 on Vercel's site, so those numbers could not be checked against the original and Vercel is not counted. Vercel's separate August 2026 post on the AI SDK repo describes the opposite policy: an agent reviewer can approve, but "nothing is merged without approval from a human on the AI SDK team".
- **Practitioners at unnamed companies.** Swizec Teller (19 September 2026) describes a GitHub Action that merges low-risk PRs with no review: 22 of 143 PRs so far. The rules are no public interface changes, no migrations, human-authored, all checks green, no finance code and no review comments.
- **An academic study.** A CMU and Stanford team (arXiv 2607.01904) followed 196,212 PRs at one unnamed company from January 2024 to April 2026. The share of PRs getting at least one human review fell from 89% to 68% while automated AI review rose from about 19% to 84%, and merge and revert rates stayed stable. Late in the window the company began routing PRs through AI review and auto-approval.
- **Before AI.** Meta's risk score was first built to let low-risk diffs land during code freezes, according to the RADAR paper. *Software Engineering at Google* (chapter 22) describes global reviewers who use pattern-based tooling to "automatically approve" large-scale changes that meet their expectations.
- **Vendor products.** GitHub announced on 1 September 2026 that Copilot code review can approve PRs, off by default, counting toward required approvals and dismissed on new commits. Greptile's auto-approve is in beta and only approves a clean 5/5 review under a risk cap. Others (Macroscope, Cubic, Cursor) were not read.

```{=html}
<div id="tip" role="tooltip"></div><script>
(function(){
  var tip=document.getElementById('tip');
  function show(e,t){tip.textContent=t;tip.style.opacity=1;var x=e.clientX+14,y=e.clientY+14;
    var w=tip.offsetWidth,h=tip.offsetHeight;if(x+w>innerWidth-8)x=innerWidth-w-8;if(y+h>innerHeight-8)y=e.clientY-h-12;
    tip.style.left=x+'px';tip.style.top=y+'px';}
  document.querySelectorAll('[data-tip]').forEach(function(el){
    el.addEventListener('mousemove',function(e){show(e,el.dataset.tip)});
    el.addEventListener('mouseleave',function(){tip.style.opacity=0});
    el.addEventListener('focus',function(){var r=el.getBoundingClientRect();show({clientX:r.left,clientY:r.bottom},el.dataset.tip)});
    el.addEventListener('blur',function(){tip.style.opacity=0});
  });
  var sel=null;
  function fill(b){
    var d=b.closest('.viz').querySelector('.detail');
    if(sel)sel.classList.remove('sel');sel=b;b.classList.add('sel');d.classList.remove('empty');
    d.innerHTML='';var h=document.createElement('div');h.className='dh';h.textContent=b.dataset.s+' · '+b.dataset.t;
    var m=document.createElement('div');m.className='dm';m.textContent=b.dataset.l;
    var p=document.createElement('div');p.textContent=b.dataset.n;d.appendChild(h);d.appendChild(m);d.appendChild(p);}
  document.querySelectorAll('button.cell').forEach(function(b){
    b.addEventListener('click',function(){fill(b)});
    b.addEventListener('mouseenter',function(){fill(b)});
  });
})();
</script>
```
